lessons.summary: Use system boundaries, inputs, outputs and interactions to explain complex scientific behaviour.
objectives: Define a useful system boundary.
Construct and critique models.
Explain feedback and interaction across components.
keyIdeas: A system model simplifies reality for a purpose.
Changing the boundary changes which transfers are counted.
A useful model states both what it represents and what it omits.

definitions.meaning: The chosen division between the system being studied and its surroundings.
A purposeful representation used to describe, explain or predict.
A process in which a system output influences later system behaviour.

method: State the question the model must answer.
Choose a boundary and label inputs, stores, transfers and outputs.
Trace one causal pathway.
Identify an assumption and testable limitation.

workedExample.prompt: Model a closed bottle terrarium as a system.
steps: Boundary: the sealed bottle.
Energy enters mainly as light and leaves mainly as thermal radiation.
Matter cycles among organisms, water, gases and soil inside the boundary.
workedExample.conclusion: The terrarium is approximately closed to matter but open to energy; the model ignores small leaks and long-term material changes.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling a model wrong because it omits detail.
misconceptions.correction: Judge whether omitted detail matters for the model’s stated purpose.

misconceptions.mistake: Confusing a system diagram with a causal explanation.
misconceptions.correction: Use labelled arrows and explain the mechanism behind each important link.

practice.prompt: For a kettle heating water, identify one energy input, one store and one output.
hints: Follow energy across the boundary.
solution: Input: electrical energy transfer.
Store: thermal energy of the water.
Output: thermal transfer to surroundings.

practice.prompt: Develop a simple model of carbon movement between plants, animals and the atmosphere.
hints: Use process labels on arrows.
solution: Atmospheric carbon dioxide enters plants through photosynthesis.
Carbon moves to animals through feeding.
Respiration returns carbon dioxide to the atmosphere.
Decomposition provides another return pathway.

practice.prompt: Evaluate a model that predicts lake temperature using only daily air temperature.
hints: Name what it captures and what it misses.
solution: Air temperature is relevant and easy to measure.
The model omits solar radiation, depth, mixing, inflows and time lag.
It may track broad seasonal change but is weak for short-term or depth-specific prediction.

practice.prompt: A sealed transparent bottle receives sunlight and loses thermal energy but no matter. Classify it as open, closed or isolated and justify.
hints: Matter and energy transfers are different.
Sealed does not mean thermally isolated.
solution: It is closed because no matter crosses the boundary.
It is not isolated because light and thermal energy cross the boundary.

practice.prompt: For a boundary around a battery and lamp together, is energy passed from battery to lamp a new external input?
hints: Locate both objects relative to the boundary.
Do not double-count internal transfers.
solution: The battery-to-lamp transfer occurs within the combined system.
It is an internal transfer; energy leaving as light or heat crosses the external boundary.

checklist: I state the purpose and limitation of a model.

notes.title: Changing the boundary changes the account
paragraphs: A system boundary determines which transfers count as inputs and outputs. The same object can be studied at several scales: a motor alone, a motor lifting a load, or the entire room. Energy transferred from a motor to a load crosses the first boundary but stays inside the second. An open system exchanges matter and energy; a closed system can exchange energy while retaining matter. A model is useful when its omissions are appropriate to the question. Drawing a boundary clearly prevents counting an internal transfer as a new input or forgetting a transfer to the surroundings.

workedExamples.prompt: A motor receives 100 J electrical energy, transfers 70 J to a lifted load and 30 J to surroundings. Compare boundaries around the motor alone and motor plus load.
steps: For the motor alone, 100 J enters while 70 J and 30 J leave by different routes.
For motor plus load, the 70 J transfer is internal and raises the load’s gravitational store; 30 J leaves the combined system.
workedExamples.conclusion: The boundary changes the accounting labels, not the total energy balance.

flashcards.front: What sets whether a transfer is internal?
flashcards.back: The chosen system boundary.

flashcards.front: Can a closed system exchange energy?
flashcards.back: Yes; closed refers to no matter transfer.
Neither matter nor energy crosses its boundary.
They determine which questions the model can answer reliably.

diagrams.title: Changing the boundary changes the account
diagrams.description: The motor-to-load transfer is internal to the larger system.

nodes.label: Motor and load
nodes.detail: 70 J raises the load’s gravitational store

edges.label: energy passes into the motor and load
account for the remaining outward transfer

lessons.summary: Track matter and energy through physical, chemical and biological systems using explicit boundaries.
objectives: Define a system boundary.
Distinguish matter transfer from energy transfer.
Use conservation reasoning across disciplines.
keyIdeas: Matter is rearranged in ordinary physical and chemical processes.
Energy transfers between stores and tends to spread into surroundings.
A conservation claim is meaningful only after the system is defined.

definitions.meaning: The chosen objects or region being analysed.
Everything outside the chosen system that can interact with it.
A quantity remains constant for an isolated system although its form or location may change.

method: Draw the system boundary.
List inputs, outputs and internal changes.
Track matter separately from energy.
Explain any apparent loss by identifying an unmeasured transfer.

workedExample.prompt: A sealed flask reaction cools while total measured mass stays constant.
steps: The sealed flask prevents matter exchange.
Reactant atoms are rearranged into products, so mass is conserved.
Cooling indicates thermal energy transferred from the reacting system to the surroundings.
workedExample.conclusion: Matter remains inside while energy crosses the chosen system boundary.

misconceptions.correction: Track where energy is transferred and how it becomes less useful or more dispersed.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating a decrease in measured mass as automatic evidence against conservation.
misconceptions.correction: Check whether gas or material crossed an open boundary.

practice.prompt: For a charging phone, identify one energy input, one useful transfer and one transfer to surroundings.
hints: Name stores or pathways.
solution: Electrical energy enters.
Energy is transferred into the battery chemical store.
Some energy is transferred thermally to the surroundings.

practice.prompt: Explain why burning fuel in an open container may leave less solid mass without violating conservation.
hints: Track gaseous products.
solution: Atoms in the fuel react with oxygen.
Gaseous products leave the measured container.
Mass is conserved for a larger closed system including gases and surrounding air.

practice.prompt: Design a measurement plan for the efficiency of a small electric water heater.
hints: Measure energy supplied and useful heating.
solution: Measure voltage, current and time for input energy.
Measure water mass and temperature change for useful energy.
Control insulation and starting conditions, repeat trials, then calculate useful/input × 100%.

practice.prompt: A hypothetical material has latent heat 150 kJ/kg. Find the energy required to melt 0.40 kg at its melting temperature.
hints: Use mass multiplied by latent heat.
Keep kilojoules throughout.
solution: The required energy is 60 kJ under the stated ideal model.

practice.prompt: A liquid boils at a steady temperature while a heater continues supplying energy. Why is “no energy is being transferred” incorrect?
hints: Energy can change state without raising temperature.
Particles separate further in the gas state.
solution: Energy is used for vaporisation and may also transfer to surroundings.
Constant temperature during the phase change does not imply zero energy input.

checklist: I track matter and energy separately.
I identify transfers rather than losses.
I choose measurements that match the claim.

notes.title: Melting separates energy transfer from temperature rise
paragraphs: Heating does not always raise temperature. During a change of state at constant pressure, supplied energy can change particle arrangement while temperature stays approximately constant. The specific latent heat connects energy to the mass changing state through E = mL. This energy account differs from E = mcΔT, which describes a temperature change within a suitable single phase. In a real experiment, containers and surroundings may also receive energy. A plateau on a temperature–time graph therefore needs a particle-level explanation and a defined system; it does not mean that energy transfer has stopped.

workedExamples.prompt: A supplied model gives ice’s latent heat of fusion as 334 kJ/kg. Find the energy needed to melt 0.20 kg ice already at its melting temperature, ignoring other transfers.
steps: Use E = mL because the phase changes without a temperature rise.
workedExamples.conclusion: The energy changes the state; it is not calculated from a non-zero temperature change.

flashcards.back: Energy transferred per mass during a specified change of state.
E = mL.

flashcards.front: Why can temperature stay constant while heating?
flashcards.back: Energy changes particle arrangement during the phase change.
Energy associated with a temperature change within the stated model.

diagrams.title: Melting separates energy transfer from temperature rise
diagrams.description: Energy changes state while the melting temperature remains approximately fixed.

lessons.summary: Use force and energy models together to explain a change, while keeping their quantities and system boundaries distinct.
objectives: Relate resultant force to acceleration in a stated model.
Account for the same motion using energy transfers.
Explain how different models answer different questions about one system.
explanation: A force model describes interactions and their effects on motion. For constant mass in a suitable reference frame, the resultant force determines acceleration through F = ma. An energy model describes stores and transfers across a chosen boundary. The two accounts can describe the same event, but force and energy are different quantities with different units. A force can act while its associated work through a particular displacement is zero.

Consider a battery-powered trolley. Chemical changes in its power source support electrical and mechanical transfers, while contact forces determine its acceleration. Some input energy increases internal energy in components and surroundings. A useful explanation connects these processes without equating battery energy directly with kinetic energy unless the missing transfers are negligible. Always state whether rolling parts, drag and other interactions are included in the simplified account.
keyIdeas: A force model and an energy model should give compatible predictions.
Net force and work by an individual force are different quantities.
A model’s omitted processes limit its prediction.

definitions.meaning: The vector sum of forces acting on the selected object or system.
The chosen division between included components and their surroundings.
A stated simplification that determines when a prediction can be applied.

method: Define the object or system and its initial state.
Identify the resultant force and relevant motion assumptions.
Account for work and energy changes using the same interval.
Compare predictions and identify transfers omitted by the simple model.

workedExample.prompt: A 2 kg block starts from rest on a frictionless horizontal surface. A constant horizontal force of 4 N acts over 3 m. Compare force and energy predictions of its final speed.
steps: The acceleration is F/m = 4/2 = 2 m/s².
For constant acceleration along this line, u is initial velocity, v final velocity and s displacement. Using v² = u² + 2as gives v² = 0 + 2 × 2 × 3 = 12, so v ≈ 3.46 m/s.
Work = Fs = 4 × 3 = 12 J. Setting ½mv² = 12 gives v² = 12 again.
workedExample.conclusion: Both accounts predict about 3.46 m/s because they use compatible assumptions. The block has no wheel rotation, and the normal force and weight do no work through the horizontal displacement.

misconceptions.mistake: Equating a force of 4 N with an energy of 4 J.
misconceptions.correction: Work also depends on displacement and relative direction.

misconceptions.mistake: Using an energy balance that omits losses while including friction in the force model.
misconceptions.correction: Use consistent system boundaries and physical assumptions in both accounts.

practice.prompt: A 3 kg block has a constant resultant horizontal force of 6 N. Find its acceleration.
hints: Use resultant force divided by mass.

practice.prompt: A 1 kg block begins at rest and gains 8 J of kinetic energy. Calculate its speed and explain why an 8 J battery input would not necessarily give the same result.
hints: First use the stated kinetic energy, then examine the input-energy assumption.
solution: 8 = ½ × 1 × v², so v = 4 m/s.
Battery input can also increase internal energy or drive other processes.
Only if the entire 8 J became the block’s translational kinetic energy would that input alone justify the same speed.

practice.prompt: A trolley moves in a straight line at constant speed while its motor continues using electrical energy. Explain why this does not contradict either the force or energy model.
hints: Straight-line constant speed means constant velocity. Turning would change velocity even at constant speed.
solution: At constant velocity the driving force balances opposing forces, giving zero resultant force.
Kinetic energy stays constant while electrical energy can be transferred to internal energy and the surroundings.
A non-zero input can therefore maintain motion without increasing kinetic energy.

practice.prompt: A 1 kg cart has speed 6 m/s and is stopped by a constant 3 N force. Find kinetic energy and braking distance.
hints: Calculate ½mv² first.
Divide energy by opposing force.
solution: Kinetic energy = ½ × 1 × 36 = 18 J.
Braking distance = 18/3 = 6 m under the model assumptions.

practice.prompt: Two identical carts brake with the same constant force, one from 3 m/s and the other from 6 m/s. Compare braking distances.
hints: Kinetic energy depends on speed squared.
Force remains unchanged.
solution: The faster cart has four times the kinetic energy.
Because distance equals energy divided by force, its braking distance is four times larger.

checklist: I distinguish force and energy units.
I account for transfers outside kinetic energy.

notes.title: Braking transfers kinetic energy
paragraphs: Braking connects a force model with an energy model. A resultant force opposite velocity reduces speed, while work done by the braking force transfers kinetic energy to other stores. For a constant opposing force, stopping distance follows from Fd = ½mv². Doubling speed therefore quadruples braking distance if mass and braking force stay fixed. This relationship concerns the braking interval only; a full stopping distance also includes the distance travelled before braking starts. Surface conditions, force changes and slopes can alter the simple prediction, so a calculation should state its assumptions.

workedExamples.prompt: A 2 kg trolley travels at 4 m/s and stops under a constant 8 N opposing force on a level track. Find braking distance.
steps: Initial kinetic energy = ½ × 2 × 4² = 16 J.
Using Fd = 16 J gives d = 16/8 = 2 m.
workedExamples.conclusion: This neglects other work and assumes a constant braking force.

flashcards.front: What energy is reduced during braking?
flashcards.back: Kinetic energy.

flashcards.front: What equation gives work by a constant parallel force?
flashcards.back: W = Fd.

flashcards.front: How does doubling speed affect ideal braking distance?
flashcards.back: It quadruples it with unchanged mass and braking force.

flashcards.front: Does braking distance include reaction distance?
flashcards.back: No; these are separate parts of stopping distance.

diagrams.title: Braking transfers kinetic energy
diagrams.description: The work of an opposing force removes the trolley’s kinetic energy.

nodes.label: Stopped trolley
nodes.detail: Kinetic energy zero; 16 J transferred elsewhere

edges.label: force does negative work on motion

lessons.summary: Explain a living system through matter exchange, chemical transformation and energy transfer at connected scales.
objectives: Trace the sources of matter used in plant growth.
Distinguish photosynthesis from cellular respiration.
Connect cell processes to an organism’s mass and energy balance.
explanation: Living organisms are open systems that exchange matter and energy with their surroundings. In a growing green plant, carbon from atmospheric carbon dioxide contributes to organic material, while water and mineral ions supply other necessary matter. Light provides energy for photosynthesis; it is not a material ingredient whose mass is simply added to the plant. Soil supports and supplies resources, but plant dry-mass gain cannot generally be equated with soil mass lost.

Photosynthesis and cellular respiration are different processes. Photosynthesis can store transferred light energy in chemical forms, while respiration transfers energy from organic substrates into usable cellular forms. Plants respire as well as photosynthesise. A measurement of net gas exchange combines processes and therefore does not directly equal the gross rate of either one. The interpretation depends on light conditions, the chosen boundary and which substances were measured.
keyIdeas: Living systems exchange matter and energy.
Light supplies energy while carbon dioxide supplies carbon.
A net measurement combines simultaneous processes.

definitions.meaning: A system that can exchange both matter and energy with its surroundings.
A process that uses light energy to form organic substances from inorganic sources, with oxygen released in the familiar plant model.
The overall measured transfer after opposing processes have been combined.

method: Define the organism or smaller system being measured.
List matter inputs, outputs and changes in stored matter.
Trace the energy supply and chemical transformations separately.
Interpret measured net changes in terms of the processes that could contribute.

workedExample.prompt: A simplified plant model fixes carbon at 9 units per hour through photosynthesis while respiration releases carbon at 4 units per hour. Find the net carbon gain and explain the limits of the model.
steps: Carbon gain from photosynthesis = 9 units per hour.
Carbon release through respiration = 4 units per hour.
Net gain = 9 - 4 = 5 units per hour.
workedExample.conclusion: The model predicts a net gain of 5 units per hour. This is a stated carbon account, not a complete fresh-mass measurement; water exchange and other carbon transfers would need separate accounting.

misconceptions.mistake: Saying a plant obtains all its growing mass from soil.
misconceptions.correction: Include carbon dioxide and water as matter sources and distinguish dry mass from fresh mass.

misconceptions.mistake: Saying plants only respire in darkness.
misconceptions.correction: Respiration occurs in light as well; light can enable photosynthesis to dominate the net exchange.

practice.prompt: Distinguish the roles of light and carbon dioxide in a green plant’s photosynthesis.
hints: Separate energy supply from a source of atoms.
solution: Light supplies energy for the process.
Carbon dioxide supplies carbon atoms used in organic substances.

practice.prompt: A simplified model gives photosynthetic carbon uptake of 12 units/hour and respiratory release of 7 units/hour. Find net uptake and explain whether zero net uptake would prove both processes had stopped.
hints: Subtract opposing transfers and consider equal non-zero rates.
solution: Net uptake = 12 - 7 = 5 units/hour.
Zero net uptake could occur if equal non-zero uptake and release balanced.
A net reading alone cannot establish that both processes are inactive.

practice.prompt: A potted plant’s fresh mass rises after watering. A learner calls the entire increase new organic biomass made by photosynthesis. Evaluate the claim.
hints: Fresh mass includes water.
solution: Water entering the plant can increase fresh mass without an equivalent increase in dry organic material.
The observation alone cannot separate water content, growth and other changes.
A suitable carbon or dry-matter account and matched measurement conditions would be needed to support the photosynthetic-biomass claim.

practice.prompt: A germinating seed in darkness releases carbon dioxide. Why does this not require photosynthesis?
hints: Seeds contain stored organic substances.
Respiration occurs without light.
solution: The seed can respire using stored food reserves.
Respiration releases carbon dioxide; photosynthesis is not required to explain this observation.

practice.prompt: A hypothetical organism takes in 12 mass units of food and oxygen during an interval, releases 9 units as measured outputs and has no other transfers. Find its mass change.
hints: Apply input minus output.
Energy transfer does not replace the matter account.
solution: Net mass change = 12 − 9 = +3 units.
Its stored mass increases by 3 units under the complete-account assumption.

checklist: I distinguish fresh and dry mass.

notes.title: Respiration connects matter and energy accounts
paragraphs: Cellular respiration transfers energy from chemical stores to processes in living cells. In the aerobic school model, glucose reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water. Atoms are rearranged rather than disappearing, and the process does not create energy from nothing. The released energy supports cell activities, with some transferred as heat. Plants as well as animals respire. Photosynthesis and respiration have related overall matter accounts, but they are different multi-step cellular processes. Measuring oxygen or carbon dioxide exchange can reveal a net balance; it does not directly measure every internal chemical step.

workedExamples.prompt: Use the word equation glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water to explain why animal mass does not simply increase by all the food eaten.
steps: Food-derived atoms can enter carbon dioxide and water during respiration.
These products can leave the body through gas exchange and other routes, while some food material is retained or excreted.
workedExamples.conclusion: A body-mass account must include outputs as well as food inputs.

flashcards.back: Yes, in light and darkness.
A suitable organic substrate such as glucose and oxygen.
No; it rearranges them into products.

flashcards.front: Why is gas exchange a net measurement?
flashcards.back: Several processes may consume or release the same gas.

diagrams.title: Respiration connects matter and energy accounts
diagrams.description: Food atoms leave in products while chemical energy supports cell activities.

nodes.label: Cellular reactions
nodes.detail: Atoms rearrange and energy is transferred

lessons.summary: Use reservoirs, flows and energy balance to connect physical, chemical and biological changes in the environment.
objectives: Distinguish a stored quantity from a transfer rate.
Construct a simple reservoir balance.
Separate an environmental mechanism from attribution of one observation.
explanation: An environmental reservoir stores matter, while a flow transfers matter between reservoirs. A carbon diagram can include atmosphere, organisms, oceans and soils, with photosynthesis, respiration and other processes connecting them. The amount stored and the rate transferred use different units. A reservoir can grow even when its outward flow is large if the inward flow is larger still.

Energy balance provides another connected account. Absorbed incoming radiation and outgoing energy influence changes in Earth’s stored energy, while chemical composition and biological processes can influence those transfers. A local observation such as one warm day does not determine a long-term global trend. Interpretation requires the appropriate spatial scale, time interval, measurements and alternative influences, rather than substituting one isolated observation for a system-level account.
keyIdeas: A stock is an amount; a flow is an amount per time.
Net change depends on inputs minus outputs.
The scale of evidence must match the scale of the claim.

definitions.meaning: A component of a system that stores a specified substance or quantity.
Transfer of a specified quantity between system components over time.
An account comparing energy inputs, outputs and change in stored energy.

method: Name the stored substance or energy and define the boundary.
Label reservoirs and flows with compatible units.
Calculate net change over the stated interval.
Connect the model to measurements at the appropriate scale and state omissions.

workedExample.prompt: A hypothetical reservoir starts with 200 tonnes of carbon. Constant annual inputs total 30 tonnes and outputs total 24 tonnes. Find its modelled amount after three years, assuming no other flows.
steps: Net annual input = 30 - 24 = 6 tonnes/year.
Three-year change = 6 × 3 = 18 tonnes.
Final amount = 200 + 18 = 218 tonnes.
workedExample.conclusion: The reservoir reaches 218 tonnes in this constant-flow model. This is an illustrative balance, not a measured forecast; changing flows would require a revised calculation.

misconceptions.mistake: Comparing 200 tonnes directly with 30 tonnes/year as if they were the same quantity.
misconceptions.correction: Distinguish amount from rate and use a time interval to connect them.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating one local measurement as proof of a global long-term change.
misconceptions.correction: Match the spatial and temporal coverage of evidence to the claim.

practice.prompt: Classify 50 tonnes of carbon and 8 tonnes of carbon per year as stock or flow.
hints: Look for the time denominator.
solution: 50 tonnes is a stock or stored amount.
8 tonnes/year is a flow rate.

practice.prompt: A model reservoir starts at 80 units, receives 11 units/day and loses 14 units/day. Find the amount after five days with constant flows and no other transfers.
hints: Keep the sign of the net change.
solution: Net rate = 11 - 14 = -3 units/day.
Five-day change = -3 × 5 = -15 units.
Final amount = 80 - 15 = 65 units.

practice.prompt: A pond’s dissolved carbon dioxide falls over one sunny afternoon. Evaluate the claim that photosynthesis is the only possible cause.
hints: The pond exchanges matter through several routes.
solution: Photosynthesis could consume dissolved carbon dioxide, but gas exchange, water movement and other chemical or biological processes can also affect the measurement.
Compare light conditions, temperature, flows and repeated measurements within a defined boundary.
The observation supports a net change, not unique attribution to one process.

practice.prompt: A surface reflects 25% of 400 incoming energy units and transmits none. Find reflected and absorbed energy.
hints: Calculate the reflected fraction first.
Subtract reflection from incoming energy.
solution: Reflected energy = 0.25 × 400 = 100 units.
Absorbed energy = 400 − 100 = 300 units.

practice.prompt: Why is the sequence warming → less ice → more absorption → further warming called positive feedback rather than a beneficial effect?
hints: Positive describes direction of reinforcement.
It is not a judgement of social value.
solution: Each linked change reinforces the original warming.
Positive labels amplification of the deviation, not whether the outcome is desirable.

checklist: I use a stated time interval.
I match evidence to the claim’s scale.

notes.title: Ice–albedo feedback can amplify warming
paragraphs: Earth-system models connect absorbed sunlight, reflected sunlight and outgoing thermal radiation. Albedo is the fraction of incoming radiation reflected by a surface. A brighter surface can reflect a larger fraction, leaving less energy absorbed under otherwise identical conditions. Feedback occurs when an initial change alters processes that amplify or oppose that change. A simplified ice–albedo feedback links warming to less ice, lower reflectivity and greater absorption. This is one mechanism within a larger system; clouds, circulation and other energy transfers also matter, so one local surface observation cannot determine the entire planet’s future temperature.

workedExamples.prompt: A surface receives 200 energy units of sunlight. Its reflected fraction changes from 0.60 to 0.30. Find absorbed energy before and after, ignoring transmission.
steps: Initially reflected energy is 120 units, so absorption is 200 − 120 = 80.
Later reflection is 60 units, so absorption is 140.
workedExamples.conclusion: Absorption rises by 60 units under unchanged incoming radiation.

flashcards.back: The fraction of incoming radiation reflected.

flashcards.front: What does lower albedo imply with fixed incoming radiation?
flashcards.back: Greater absorption if transmission is unchanged or negligible.
It amplifies the initial change.

flashcards.front: Is one feedback a complete climate model?
flashcards.back: No; other processes also affect the energy balance.

diagrams.title: Ice–albedo feedback can amplify warming
diagrams.description: This simplified loop describes one contribution to a larger climate system.

nodes.label: Additional warming
nodes.detail: The initial temperature change is amplified

lessons.summary: Design a comparison that connects scientific models while measuring the outcome relevant to the question.
objectives: Choose a measurable outcome for an interdisciplinary claim.
Identify independent treatment units and competing influences.
Explain how controls and repeated observations strengthen a comparison.
explanation: An interdisciplinary question may involve several mechanisms, but it still needs a clear testable claim. A covering around a cup might change heat transfer, absorb water or alter evaporation. Before collecting data, decide whether the claim concerns cooling rate, moisture movement or another outcome. Measuring one convenient signal does not automatically test every advertised benefit of a material.

Define which unit independently receives each condition and which variables should remain consistent. Several temperature readings from one cup trace its cooling curve; they do not replace several independently prepared cups when estimating variation between trials. Choose a classroom-approved procedure with suitable low-risk materials, consistent instruments and a planned analysis. Record unexpected observations because they may reveal a competing process that the original model omitted.
keyIdeas: The measured response must match the claim.
One object’s time series is different from independent trial replication.
Unexpected observations can reveal a missing mechanism.

definitions.meaning: The measured outcome used to examine the effect of a condition.
A relevant influence kept consistent to make the intended comparison interpretable.
Use of independently prepared or assigned units to assess variation in the comparison.

method: State one specific claim and its measured response.
Identify the experimental unit and competing mechanisms.
Plan controls, independent replicates and consistent measurement times.
Record all observations and compare them with the stated model.

workedExample.prompt: Plan a conceptual classroom comparison of two cup coverings claimed to reduce cooling. The teacher supplies an approved warm-water procedure.
steps: Use temperature change over a fixed interval as the response for the cooling claim.
Keep cup type, water amount, starting temperature, room conditions and measurement timing consistent.
Prepare independent cups for each covering and allocate positions to reduce location bias.
Record temperatures and any moisture loss or covering changes that could affect interpretation.
workedExample.conclusion: The design tests cooling under the stated conditions. It does not by itself establish a material’s strength, overall environmental benefit or performance at every temperature.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating many time readings from one cup as many independent treatment trials.
misconceptions.correction: Use independently prepared treatment units to estimate between-trial variation.

misconceptions.mistake: Claiming one successful temperature test validates every property of a material.
misconceptions.correction: Match each claim to relevant measurements and conditions.

practice.prompt: For a cup-covering cooling comparison, identify a response variable and two relevant controls.
hints: Choose the cooling outcome and factors that could also change it.
solution: A response is temperature decrease over a stated interval.
Relevant controls include water amount, starting temperature, cup type and room conditions.

practice.prompt: One covered cup is read every minute for ten minutes. Explain what these ten readings establish and what they do not establish about trial-to-trial variation.
hints: Distinguish a time series from independent treatment units.
solution: The readings describe the temperature pattern within that cup over time.
They do not measure variation among ten independently prepared covered cups.
Independent repeated trials are needed to assess how consistently the condition performs.

practice.prompt: Covering A starts with hotter water than covering B. After ten minutes A is still hotter, so a learner declares it the better insulator. Evaluate the conclusion.
hints: Final temperature also depends on the starting condition.
solution: Different starting temperatures confound the comparison, so the final readings alone do not isolate the coverings’ effects.
Use matched starting conditions and compare the planned cooling response across independent trials.
Consider other transfers, including evaporation, before attributing the result solely to insulation.

practice.prompt: In a panel-colour warming study, identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one relevant control.
hints: Colour is deliberately changed.
The response must include a time interval.
solution: Independent variable: panel colour; dependent variable: temperature rise over a fixed interval.
A relevant control is panel material, thickness or lamp distance.

practice.prompt: A black metal panel warms more than a white wooden panel. Does the result isolate colour?
hints: Two material properties changed together.
Construct a comparison with one intended factor.
solution: Colour and material differ, so absorption and thermal properties are confounded.
Use otherwise matched panels differing only in the intended surface colour and document finish.

notes.title: Surface absorption changes temperature
paragraphs: An interdisciplinary experiment should identify the mechanism linking a changed factor to an observed outcome. A study of surface colour and warming, for example, connects light absorption to thermal energy transfer. Colour should vary while material, thickness, illuminated area and starting conditions remain comparable. Position matters if the light source illuminates unevenly, so locations can be randomised or exchanged systematically across independent trials. Record the temperature change over a fixed interval instead of comparing unrelated final temperatures. A convincing design also names limitations, such as differences in surface finish that may accompany colour changes.

workedExamples.prompt: Plan a teacher-approved comparison of warming in two coloured panels under the same lamp.
steps: Use panels of the same material, size and thickness with matched initial temperatures and lamp distances.
Measure temperature change over a fixed interval, and randomise panel positions across independent trials.
workedExamples.conclusion: Surface finish remains a possible difference to document or control.

flashcards.front: What is the response in a warming comparison?
flashcards.back: Temperature change over a specified interval.
Final temperature depends on the initial condition.
Illumination may vary by location.

flashcards.front: What material factor can confound colour?
flashcards.back: Thickness, composition or surface finish.

diagrams.title: Surface absorption changes temperature
diagrams.description: The design links a physical mechanism to a measured response.

nodes.label: Surface absorption
nodes.detail: Colour and finish affect absorbed energy

edges.label: part of the light is absorbed

lessons.summary: Combine measurements across scientific contexts while retaining units, uncertainty and the limits of a summary.
objectives: Calculate a derived quantity with matching units.
Use stated endpoint uncertainty bounds in a simple difference.
Distinguish measurement limits from natural variation and model limitations.
explanation: Data from different sciences can be combined only when their quantities and conditions are compatible. A temperature difference is not a heat transfer until mass and heat capacity are included in a suitable model. A concentration is not a total mass without a volume or other denominator. Write the relationship and units before substituting numbers so that an attractive but meaningless numerical comparison does not replace a physical account.

Uncertainty can arise from instruments, the measurement procedure and variation among samples. A derived result inherits relevant measurement limits, while a model may add further assumptions. For an introductory worst-case interval calculation, endpoint bounds can be combined conservatively; this is different from a statistical confidence interval. Repeated readings help describe variation but do not automatically remove a shared instrument offset or establish that the model is complete.
keyIdeas: A derived quantity needs a stated relationship and units.
Different kinds of uncertainty should be named.
Conservative endpoint bounds are not statistical confidence claims.

definitions.meaning: A quantity calculated from other measurements using a stated relationship.
An estimate describing limits on a measured value under specified conditions.
A restriction arising from an omitted process or simplified relationship rather than measurement alone.

method: Identify the measured and derived quantities with units.
Write the relationship and its assumptions.
Apply the stated uncertainty convention consistently.
Report the result with appropriate precision and distinguish unaccounted limitations.

workedExample.prompt: A temperature falls from 30.0 ± 0.2°C to 24.0 ± 0.2°C. Treat these as endpoint bounds and find the nominal fall and conservative possible range, without assuming error cancellation.
steps: Nominal fall = 30.0 - 24.0 = 6.0°C.
Smallest fall = 29.8 - 24.2 = 5.6°C.
Largest fall = 30.2 - 23.8 = 6.4°C.
workedExample.conclusion: The conservative endpoint result is a 6.0 ± 0.4°C fall. This interval follows the supplied bounds; correlated errors or a different uncertainty model would need separate treatment.

misconceptions.mistake: Adding more decimal places to imply greater measurement certainty.
misconceptions.correction: Report precision consistent with the stated uncertainty.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating a model assumption as if it were measured instrument uncertainty.
misconceptions.correction: Explain omitted processes separately from limits on the observations.

practice.prompt: A sample has 6 mg of a substance in 2 L. Calculate concentration and explain why 6 mg and 3 mg/L are not interchangeable descriptions.
hints: One is an amount; the other includes volume.
solution: Concentration = 6/2 = 3 mg/L.
6 mg is total substance mass; 3 mg/L is mass per unit volume.

practice.prompt: Two readings are 18.0 ± 0.1 cm and 12.0 ± 0.1 cm. Using conservative endpoint bounds without assumed cancellation, find their positive difference and interval.
hints: Subtract the largest second reading from the smallest first reading for the lower bound.
solution: Nominal difference = 18.0 - 12.0 = 6.0 cm.
Lower bound = 17.9 - 12.1 = 5.8 cm; upper bound = 18.1 - 11.9 = 6.2 cm.
The stated endpoint result is 6.0 ± 0.2 cm.

practice.prompt: A heat-transfer calculation uses repeated precise temperatures but ignores energy absorbed by the container. Explain why more temperature readings alone may not fix the result.
hints: Separate measurement repeatability from an omitted energy pathway.
solution: Repeated readings can improve knowledge of temperature variation.
Ignoring container heating leaves an incomplete energy model even if temperature readings are precise.
Include the relevant container energy transfer or justify its negligible size before claiming a complete heat balance.

practice.prompt: A volume increases by 40 mL in 8 s. Find average rate and explain whether this proves the instantaneous rate was constant.
hints: Divide total change by total time.
An average does not show the shape within the interval.
solution: Average rate = 40/8 = 5 mL/s.
The instantaneous rate could vary while producing the same total; intermediate readings are needed.

practice.prompt: A mass is bounded between 18 and 22 g and volume between 4 and 5 cm³. Find conservative density bounds.
hints: Density is mass divided by volume.
Pair the smallest mass with largest volume for the minimum.
solution: Minimum density = 18/5 = 3.6 g/cm³.
Maximum density = 22/4 = 5.5 g/cm³.

checklist: I separate measurement limits from model assumptions.

notes.title: Rate bounds combine both measurements
paragraphs: Derived rates inherit uncertainty from both the measured change and the elapsed time. When bounds are supplied, the smallest ratio uses the smallest numerator with the largest positive denominator; the largest ratio uses the opposite endpoints. This produces a conservative range under the stated bounding model, not a statistical confidence interval. Units must be carried through the calculation. Rounding intermediate values too early can distort the final range, so retain enough digits until reporting. Measurement uncertainty should also be distinguished from model omissions, such as assuming a constant rate when only the total change was measured.

workedExamples.prompt: A distance is 10.0 ± 0.2 m and time is 2.0 ± 0.1 s, treated as bounds. Find nominal average speed and endpoint range.
steps: Nominal speed = 10.0/2.0 = 5.0 m/s.
workedExamples.conclusion: The conservative range is about 4.67–5.37 m/s, not a confidence claim.

flashcards.front: How is the smallest positive ratio bounded?
flashcards.back: Smallest numerator divided by largest denominator.
Distance and elapsed time.

flashcards.front: Does a bound imply a confidence level?
flashcards.back: No, unless a statistical interpretation is separately supplied.
It can change the final calculated bounds.

diagrams.title: Rate bounds combine both measurements
diagrams.description: Opposite endpoints produce the extreme positive ratios.

lessons.summary: Evaluate an interdisciplinary claim by checking the evidence for each link and separating measured outcomes from broader judgements.
objectives: Break a broad claim into testable components.
Identify evidence that would distinguish competing explanations.
Give a qualified conclusion while retaining negative or inconclusive findings.
explanation: A broad claim such as “this material is better for the environment” combines several questions. Physical performance, chemical persistence, biological effects and resource use may require different measurements. Evidence supporting one component does not automatically establish all the others. Begin by identifying the comparison, time horizon, system boundary and meaning of better before deciding what the data can support.

A credible evaluation follows each causal link. If a material changes appearance in water, the observation does not by itself show complete biodegradation or harmless products. If a device uses less energy during operation, its production and disposal may still matter to a wider assessment. Report what was measured, what remains unknown and which further evidence would resolve the uncertainty. Negative results can constrain a claim even when they do not suggest a preferred alternative.
keyIdeas: Broad claims contain several distinct evidence requirements.
Visible change does not uniquely identify a chemical or biological process.
A qualified conclusion can support one claim while leaving another unresolved.

definitions.meaning: The linked observations and reasoning needed to support a multi-step claim.
The stages of production, use and disposal included in an assessment.
A situation where improving one relevant outcome can worsen another.

method: Break the claim into measurable components.
Match each component to relevant evidence and a comparison.
Check alternative explanations, boundary choices and uncertainty.
State the supported conclusion and unresolved questions separately.

workedExample.prompt: A reusable cup requires 100 energy units to produce and 2 units to wash per use. A disposable alternative requires 6 units per use. In this simplified equal-service model, find when the reusable option uses less total energy.
steps: Reusable energy after n uses = 100 + 2n; disposable energy = 6n.
For a lower reusable total, 100 + 2n < 6n, so n > 25.
At 25 uses both totals are 150 units; from 26 whole uses, the reusable total is lower.
workedExample.conclusion: The break-even point is 25 uses under the supplied energy-only assumptions. This does not establish total environmental superiority because water use, transport, materials, disposal and actual service life are outside the model.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating success on one metric as proof of overall superiority.
misconceptions.correction: State the criteria and assess the other relevant outcomes.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling fragmentation complete biodegradation from appearance alone.
misconceptions.correction: Identify the transformation and products with appropriate evidence rather than relying on visible breakup.

practice.prompt: A lamp uses less electricity during use. Name one supported observation and one broader claim that needs more evidence.
hints: Separate the measured use phase from a whole-life judgement.
solution: The supplied observation supports lower use-phase electricity under the measured conditions.
A claim of lower total environmental impact needs evidence about other stages and relevant impacts.

practice.prompt: Option A uses 60 energy units to produce and 1 per use. Option B uses 4 units per use. Find the equal-energy use count and the first whole use at which A is lower, assuming equal service and no other energy costs.
hints: Set 60 + n equal to 4n, then check strict inequality.
solution: 60 + n = 4n gives n = 20 uses, when both totals are 80 units.
A is lower when n > 20, so the first whole use is 21.
The comparison depends on the stated production, use and service assumptions.

practice.prompt: A material breaks into small pieces in water, so a learner declares it fully biodegraded and harmless. Evaluate both parts of the claim.
hints: Appearance, chemical transformation and biological effect are different outcomes.
solution: Visible fragmentation does not establish complete biological breakdown into specified products.
Harmlessness requires relevant evidence about exposure and effects; smaller pieces alone do not prove it.
Report the observed breakup and seek evidence for transformation products and biological effects before making either broader claim.

practice.prompt: A hypothetical treatment removes 80% of 150 mg solute. Find removed and remaining masses.
hints: Multiply by 0.80 for removal.
Subtract from the initial mass.
solution: Removed mass = 0.80 × 150 = 120 mg.
Remaining mass = 150 − 120 = 30 mg.

practice.prompt: Device A uses less energy per litre than B, but A treats twice as many litres. Does lower intensity guarantee lower total energy use?
hints: Total equals intensity multiplied by service volume.
Both factors are needed.
solution: No; a larger volume can outweigh the lower energy per litre.
Compare each intensity multiplied by its actual volume, or compare equal volumes for an efficiency judgement.

checklist: I define the comparison and boundary.
I examine each link in the claim.
I preserve unresolved and negative findings.

notes.title: Removal performance has more than one measure
paragraphs: A technology can perform well on one measure while doing poorly on another. Evaluation begins by defining the service and the criteria, such as removal efficiency, energy use or maintenance demand. Percentages need a denominator: removing 90% of a small initial quantity differs from removing 90% of a large one. Comparing systems fairly may require reporting both the remaining amount and the resources used per unit of service. A weighted judgement should state whose priorities determine the weights. Evidence about performance does not, by itself, decide ethical or social questions about access, affordability or acceptable trade-offs.

workedExamples.prompt: A fictional filter treats 100 L containing 200 mg solute and removes 90%. Another treats the same input and removes 95% but uses twice the energy. Compare the supported outcomes.
steps: The first leaves 20 mg; the second leaves 10 mg.
The second removes 10 mg more but uses twice the energy for the same volume.
workedExamples.conclusion: Preference requires criteria about residual amount and energy, not removal percentage alone.

flashcards.back: Different treatment volumes or outputs can distort comparisons.
Ten per cent of the initial amount.
Improvement in one relevant outcome accompanied by a cost in another.
The stated decision-maker or affected stakeholders, with reasons made explicit.

diagrams.title: Removal performance has more than one measure
diagrams.description: A higher percentage can improve one outcome while increasing another cost.
